CargoSub_ballast.description: There are 8 ballast tanks, four each at the bow and stern. In each group, there are top, bottom, port and starboard tanks. The tanks
CargoSub_ballast.these_tanks_are_different: On a normal submarine masses vary little relative to the sub's displacement, and changes are tracked carefully. The trim balast tanks on a normal sub are very small. The main ballast tanks aren't used to modulate bouyancy. They are fully blown to surface, or fully flooded to achieve a precalculated neutral bouyancy immediately, with only minor adjustments to the trim tanks. Once submerged, the sub does very little blowing or flooding because it operates at nearly constant weight. CargoSub is completely different. It loads and unloads payloads that weight more than the sub itself. The main ballast tanks cannot sit with constant ballast. As loads are taken up or released, the ballast tanks must be exercise across much of their range of ballast. Because the payload can be greater than the sub's weight, they must take up a dramatic fraction of the sub's volume. Despite their size, they must be flooded and blown quickly, if loading and unloading are to proceed quickly. This all implies a huge need for pressurized air, and not just air at one atmosphere, but up to 60 atmospheres, to blow the tanks mostly empty, at the greatest depths, and greatest weights. Unless the charging air tanks are themselves abnormally large, CHARGING AIR IS A VALUABLE RESOURCE. It cannot be blown overboard.

ballast_tanks.description: Each tank has two fluid ports at the bottom for the exchange of seawater. There are two fluid ports at the top for the exchange of charging air. Until an optimal setup is found through testing, large fluid pumps will be used to pump air and water in and out of the tank, as the pumps may often be fighting against a back pressure. When not being pumped, the ballast tanks are generally isolated from sea chests and the charging air system. They are not free-flooding.

CargoSub_ballast.water_pump_system: Each set of tanks, fore and aft, each have two banks of water pumps. One bank pumps water inboard, the other bank pumps outboard. Valve manifolds connect to the water ports on each tank, so that tanks may be pumped in and out simultaneously. The pumps have a direct connection to fluid ports on the bottom of the sub.
CargoSub_ballast.air_pump_system: The air pumps are arranged in a similar manner to the water pumps, but do not connect to outside air. They instead connect to a massive network of charging air tanks that function as a central source to take air from, and return air to. Header tanks are supplied at the bow and stern for the air pumps to connect directly to, minimizing any lag in the system. The header tanks share a common manifold along the sub to air storage tanks scattered about the sub in ideal places. The common charging air manifold can be recharged via a breather in the snorkel when surfaced.
CargoSub_ballast.auxiliary_air_uses: Other users of charging air, like the environmental system, engineering room and airlock pressurization, etc, have their own taps into the charging air manifold.
